{"findings": [
  {"file": "pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go", "line": 51, "severity": "high", "category": "concurrency", "title": "Async legacy writes are derived from the request context and get canceled when the request returns", "body": "In Create (line 51), Update (line 135), Delete (line 110) and DeleteCollection (line 163), the background goroutine derives its context via context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...) from the ctx passed into the handler, which is the request-scoped context. The API server cancels the request context as soon as the response is written and the handler returns, so these goroutines will usually see context.Canceled almost immediately and the LegacyStorage call will abort before writing. This defeats the entire purpose of mode 3 (mirroring writes to the legacy store as a safety net): most legacy writes will silently never happen. Fix by detaching from cancellation, e.g. context.WithTimeoutCause(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), ...), while still carrying the logger values."},
  {"file": "pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go", "line": 106, "severity": "high", "category": "bug", "title": "Delete records the object name as the metric 'kind' label, creating unbounded label cardinality", "body": "On success Delete calls d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage). The third argument of recordStorageDuration is the kind label (every other call passes options.Kind), so here the object's metadata.name is used as the kind label. Object names are request/user-controlled and unbounded (generated names, arbitrary names), so this turns the storage-duration metric into a high-cardinality metric and can cause memory growth / scrape slowdowns. It should pass options.Kind."},
  {"file": "pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go", "line": 45, "severity": "medium", "category": "bug", "title": "Storage failures are recorded as legacy durations", "body": "In Create the error branch calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) even though the operation that just failed was the synchronous Storage.Create (and startStorage measures the storage call), so storage errors are attributed to the legacy-store metric. The same mistake exists in Update at line 129. Both should call recordStorageDuration with the storage timing. As-is, the storage error-rate/latency dashboards will be wrong and legacy error metrics will be inflated."},
  {"file": "pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go", "line": 166, "severity": "medium", "category": "bug", "title": "DeleteCollection records the legacy operation as a storage duration", "body": "Inside the DeleteCollection goroutine the legacy store's DeleteCollection result is recorded with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). Since startLegacy and the operation are both the legacy store, this should be recordLegacyDuration. Otherwise legacy latency/errors are counted as unified-storage metrics and the storage metric is polluted with legacy timings."},
  {"file": "pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go", "line": 56, "severity": "medium", "category": "data", "title": "Async legacy write failures are never logged, so legacy drift is invisible", "body": "After writing to storage, the goroutines call the legacy store and only feed the error into d.recordLegacyDuration(...) (Create line 56, Update line 140, Delete line 113, DeleteCollection line 166). There is no log statement on failure, unlike the previous implementation which logged 'unable to create/update/delete ... in legacy storage'. Because the legacy write is the safety net for mode 3, a persistent failure (e.g. the context cancellation above, or a real legacy error) would silently cause the legacy store to diverge from unified storage with only a boolean counter to show it. Log the error, including the object name/kind, so operators can detect and repair drift."},
  {"file": "pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3_test.go", "line": 65, "severity": "medium", "category": "test_gap", "title": "Dual-write tests never wait for or assert the async legacy write, and share one mock for both stores", "body": "TestMode3_Create (line 65) and TestMode3_Update (line 345) return as soon as the synchronous storage call completes; the background legacy goroutine is not awaited and no assertion verifies LegacyStorage was actually called. Moreover the same *mock.Mock instance is used for both legacyStoreMock and storageMock, so even AssertCalled/AssertNotCalled cannot distinguish storage calls from legacy calls. The test therefore does not exercise the core behavior of mode 3 (async mirroring to the legacy store). The leaked goroutine can also touch the shared, non-thread-safe testify mock and the shared package-level prometheus registry after the subtest has finished, producing data races under -race. Use separate mocks and synchronize on the goroutine (e.g. a channel/WaitGroup injected for tests) before asserting."},
  {"file": "pkg/tests/apis/playlist/playlist_test.go", "line": 191, "severity": "medium", "category": "test_gap", "title": "Mode 3 playlist integration tests read the legacy API immediately after k8s writes and will be flaky", "body": "The added 'with dual write (... mode 3)' subtests (lines 132-144, 191-204, 287-312) run doPlaylistTests, which performs k8s CRUD and then immediately reads back via the legacy /api/playlists endpoints (e.g. the legacy list at line 523 and getFromBothAPIs at line 623) and asserts identical results. Under mode 3 the legacy write happens asynchronously, so the legacy store may not yet reflect the k8s create/update/delete when the legacy read runs, making require.Equal on the UID/field values intermittently fail. The tests need to wait/poll for the legacy mirror (or the shared helper must account for mode 3's asynchronous write semantics)."},
  {"file": "pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go", "line": 97, "severity": "low", "category": "bug", "title": "Delete puts the bare d.Log into the context instead of the enriched logger", "body": "Delete builds log := d.Log.WithValues(\"name\", name, \"kind\", options.Kind, \"method\", method) but then calls ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log), discarding the per-request values. Every other method stores the enriched logger in the context. Downstream Storage.Delete/Legacy.Delete and their logs therefore lose the kind/method/name context that was intended. Use klog.NewContext(ctx, log)."}
]}

findings.title: Async legacy writes are derived from the request context and get canceled when the request returns
findings.body: In Create (line 51), Update (line 135), Delete (line 110) and DeleteCollection (line 163), the background goroutine derives its context via context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...) from the ctx passed into the handler, which is the request-scoped context. The API server cancels the request context as soon as the response is written and the handler returns, so these goroutines will usually see context.Canceled almost immediately and the LegacyStorage call will abort before writing. This defeats the entire purpose of mode 3 (mirroring writes to the legacy store as a safety net): most legacy writes will silently never happen. Fix by detaching from cancellation, e.g. context.WithTimeoutCause(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), ...), while still carrying the logger values.

findings.title: Delete records the object name as the metric 'kind' label, creating unbounded label cardinality
findings.body: On success Delete calls d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage). The third argument of recordStorageDuration is the kind label (every other call passes options.Kind), so here the object's metadata.name is used as the kind label. Object names are request/user-controlled and unbounded (generated names, arbitrary names), so this turns the storage-duration metric into a high-cardinality metric and can cause memory growth / scrape slowdowns. It should pass options.Kind.

findings.title: Storage failures are recorded as legacy durations
findings.body: In Create the error branch calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) even though the operation that just failed was the synchronous Storage.Create (and startStorage measures the storage call), so storage errors are attributed to the legacy-store metric. The same mistake exists in Update at line 129. Both should call recordStorageDuration with the storage timing. As-is, the storage error-rate/latency dashboards will be wrong and legacy error metrics will be inflated.

findings.title: DeleteCollection records the legacy operation as a storage duration
findings.body: Inside the DeleteCollection goroutine the legacy store's DeleteCollection result is recorded with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). Since startLegacy and the operation are both the legacy store, this should be recordLegacyDuration. Otherwise legacy latency/errors are counted as unified-storage metrics and the storage metric is polluted with legacy timings.

findings.title: Async legacy write failures are never logged, so legacy drift is invisible
findings.body: After writing to storage, the goroutines call the legacy store and only feed the error into d.recordLegacyDuration(...) (Create line 56, Update line 140, Delete line 113, DeleteCollection line 166). There is no log statement on failure, unlike the previous implementation which logged 'unable to create/update/delete ... in legacy storage'. Because the legacy write is the safety net for mode 3, a persistent failure (e.g. the context cancellation above, or a real legacy error) would silently cause the legacy store to diverge from unified storage with only a boolean counter to show it. Log the error, including the object name/kind, so operators can detect and repair drift.

findings.title: Dual-write tests never wait for or assert the async legacy write, and share one mock for both stores
findings.body: TestMode3_Create (line 65) and TestMode3_Update (line 345) return as soon as the synchronous storage call completes; the background legacy goroutine is not awaited and no assertion verifies LegacyStorage was actually called. Moreover the same *mock.Mock instance is used for both legacyStoreMock and storageMock, so even AssertCalled/AssertNotCalled cannot distinguish storage calls from legacy calls. The test therefore does not exercise the core behavior of mode 3 (async mirroring to the legacy store). The leaked goroutine can also touch the shared, non-thread-safe testify mock and the shared package-level prometheus registry after the subtest has finished, producing data races under -race. Use separate mocks and synchronize on the goroutine (e.g. a channel/WaitGroup injected for tests) before asserting.

findings.title: Mode 3 playlist integration tests read the legacy API immediately after k8s writes and will be flaky
findings.body: The added 'with dual write (... mode 3)' subtests (lines 132-144, 191-204, 287-312) run doPlaylistTests, which performs k8s CRUD and then immediately reads back via the legacy /api/playlists endpoints (e.g. the legacy list at line 523 and getFromBothAPIs at line 623) and asserts identical results. Under mode 3 the legacy write happens asynchronously, so the legacy store may not yet reflect the k8s create/update/delete when the legacy read runs, making require.Equal on the UID/field values intermittently fail. The tests need to wait/poll for the legacy mirror (or the shared helper must account for mode 3's asynchronous write semantics).

findings.title: Delete puts the bare d.Log into the context instead of the enriched logger
findings.body: Delete builds log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method) but then calls ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log), discarding the per-request values. Every other method stores the enriched logger in the context. Downstream Storage.Delete/Legacy.Delete and their logs therefore lose the kind/method/name context that was intended. Use klog.NewContext(ctx, log).
